text: Carving is taught by repetition, and the new apprentice has a prison term behind him and a trade to learn from an old man who has done nothing else. Lee Hsing keeps the town small in every sense: one workshop, one household, neighbours who know each other's hours. The sculptor's daughter does not speak, so whatever forms between her and the newcomer has to be assembled out of work, gesture and proximity, and the film slows itself to that rate deliberately. Then a local troublemaker begins circling her, and the pressure falls on the one man in town whose account of anything counts for least. The Golden Horse named it the best feature of 1979, which indicates what Taiwanese taste rewarded then: patience, handwork, a story that stays indoors and never raises its voice.

1937, and the war with Japan is a few weeks old; the subject here is the men who went up to meet it in the air. Chang Tseng-Chai works from the record of a small group of Chinese fliers through the fighting at Shanghai and then at Nanking, two names that arrive heavy before a frame has passed. A hundred minutes is not long for a campaign, and the compression shows where the interest lies: not in strategy but in the intervals on the ground, in the arithmetic of a handful of men who cannot afford losses. Four decades separate the film from the events. That is near enough that some in the 1977 audience remembered them, and far enough that the shape of the telling had settled into something an industry could stage whole.

The transaction at the centre of Chokh is legal on paper and nothing like it in any other respect: a mill owner forging documents to obtain a worker's donated eyes. His son cannot see. That is the whole of the father's reasoning, and Utpalendu Chakrabarty gives it room enough to sound almost sensible before the other half of the arrangement comes into view — a labourer framed for murders he did not commit, whose body stays useful to the mill after the mill is finished with him. Ninety-eight minutes in Bengali, made in 1981, and the National Film Award for best feature went to it. What carries is the exactness of the anger: about who signs, who witnesses, whose name is worth something at a desk, and who can be described any way at all once he has no standing to disagree.

An escape line works only because nobody asks questions, which is also what makes it simple to poison. France, 1944: an American pilot is shot down, picked up by a resistance group, and parked among strangers while the road south to Spain is arranged. One of them is a British major who says he broke out of a German camp. Rudolf Jugert plays it as a chamber piece, so the suspense sits in the waiting rather than the crossing, where the only evidence available about a man is how he behaves at close quarters. West Germany made this in 1964, which puts a German production on the far side of its own occupation, watching the trapped try to work out who among them is working for whom. Ninety-five minutes, and most of the danger is conversational.

The problem with filming a writer is that the important part happens where a camera cannot follow. Helma Sanders-Brahms spends 128 minutes with Heinrich von Kleist anyway, and the length functions as an argument: a life of this kind is not a row of incidents to be ticked off but a condition to be sat inside. Struggles, the record says, and the word covers a great deal — the hours before the writing, the hours after, whatever company was available in between. Made in West Germany in 1977, it takes a figure out of the national literature and declines to make him decorative or safely historical. Two hours and eight minutes is a long sitting for one man's difficulty. The film treats that as the minimum, not the indulgence.

Independence is the hinge, and the film watches it from inside a house rather than from the street. Girish Kasaravalli adapts Ranganath Shyamrao Lokapura's novel about a Brahmin family whose standing was arranged under one order and has to be carried into another, and the frame stays domestic throughout: rooms, obligations, the slow accounting of what is owned and what is owed. Kannada, 117 minutes, made in 1996 — half a century after the change it describes, which lets it treat the political turn as inheritance rather than as news. The interest is not in the transfer of power but in what a household does when the arrangement that made sense of it is quietly withdrawn, and in how long people keep performing duties with nothing behind them.

A man is told to fetch a tiger's mane and tail, and the only way to get them is to become a tiger. The order comes from above, from the upper castes of North Kerala and a ruler said to need curing, and it falls on Kari Gurukkal, remembered by the Pulaya community as a master of martial arts and afterwards as a god. Priyanandanan films the legend as legend and treats the transformation as a practical problem: there is a way back out of the tiger form, involving water from washed rice and a broom, and it depends entirely on somebody else performing it correctly. Eighty-seven minutes in Malayalam. The folklore is old; the arrangement underneath it is not hard to recognise — a man whose skill makes him necessary to people who will not have him in the room.

Eighty-five minutes, a sickbed, and two men who stopped speaking to each other years ago. The son comes back because his father is ill; nothing else would have brought him. What he finds is a silence with a shape to it, a remorse the old man carries and has never explained to anyone. K. S. Sethumadhavan made it in Tamil in 1989 and kept the scale to a house, an illness, and a question that can only be asked sideways. The National Film Award for best feature went to it, which for a film this small means a jury preferred the mechanics of finding something out to the drama of announcing it. Between knowing what a parent did and understanding why it was never said there is a considerable distance, and eighty-five minutes turns out to be enough of it.

Winston Churchill appears here as the police official with a siege on his hands and anarchists at the far end of the street. The anarchist is Enrico Malatesta, played by Eddie Constantine, leading a group of Latvian exiles through the events at Sidney Street, and the film's sympathies rest with him rather than with the men organising against him. Peter Lilienthal made it for German television in 1970 at eighty-six minutes, and television money does not buy a siege as spectacle, so the confrontation becomes a matter of rooms, doors and timing. Edwardian London figures mainly as the party the group is trying to reach: an aristocracy that would have to be badly startled before it would hear a demand at all. The noise is the channel; nothing quieter would have carried that far.

A poet arrives at a country parsonage in Alsace and asks a gentle man for help that no gentleness can supply. George Moorse gives Büchner's short story 130 minutes, a great deal of room for a text made almost entirely of interior weather, and the length obliges the film to live through the days rather than summarise them: the walks, the meals, the stretches when nothing is visibly wrong. Oberlin is the difficulty. Patient, generous, a philanthropist by vocation, he reads his guest's hallucinations as something God has sent, so every kindness lands slightly beside what is needed. West Germany, 1971, a Sturm und Drang poet's unravelling staged as household routine — a guest, a host, and an obligation of hospitality that neither man thinks to question.

An ensemble picture has no single hero, and for a film about a country's founding that decision carries weight. Ting Shan-Hsi spreads 121 minutes across many hands, so the political upheavals of the early twentieth century arrive as distributed work rather than as one man's biography, which is both closer to how such things happen and more flattering to everyone involved. Taiwan sent it to the Academy Awards as its entry for the year. Extravagance is part of the argument: scale is what a founding is expected to look like once a state is telling it. The interest now lies partly in the seams, at the places where the record runs out and the film's sense of how the record ought to have felt takes over.

German troops enter Prague in 1939, and the film stays inside one apartment block to watch what that does to the tenants. A widow is trying to reach the son she once disowned, with Brazil in mind; a couple's stationery shop is being dismantled by the occupiers; and the caretaker, Glaser, German by descent, is about to learn what that descent is worth and what will be asked in exchange for it. Kurt Hoffmann takes 155 minutes and lets the occupation arrive the way it arrives at an address: as licences, rent, paperwork, a knock at an inconvenient hour. It was made in West Germany in 1965 and carried the German Film Award for best feature, which placed a German production inside a Czech building at the moment German soldiers walk into it.

Five prizes at the 1976 Golden Horse, best feature among them, and an industry closing ranks around one of its own. Liu Chia-chang's film is Taiwanese, ninety-five minutes, set during the war with Japan, and it goes out in Chinese as 梅花. That runtime rules out a campaign. What fits is a portion of a war, held long enough to register, and the weight falls on tone: a conflict of that size reduces ordinary life to a series of small permissions, and a film that stages those as pageantry loses the thing it set out to show, while one that stays with them can reach it without a battle scene at all. A war is one thing while it is being fought and another once an industry has time to compose it; this one comes from the second stage.

The press is worked by hand, and the only other person in the shop is his wife. What comes off it is Jangipur Sangbad, a small-town paper that the man everyone calls Dada Thakur uses to argue against the customs of his own community and then against the people who run the district. Chhabi Biswas plays him. The film was made in 1961, while its subject was still living, which is an unusual arrangement for a biography: the man could read what was said about him and answer back. Nalini Kanta Sarkar, a freedom-fighter working underground, joins the paper; the local zamindar's son begins pursuing a girl named Lata, and the argument stops being about columns. A newspaper in a town that size is less a trade than a standing position, taken daily, in front of neighbours who know where the presses are.
